Activity preserves all component state and DOM state by default. For each piece of state, you decide whether that's the right behavior for your UI. The patterns below show common scenarios and how to handle both sides.
When a user navigates away and returns, Activity preserves the open/closed state of expandable elements.
A sidebar with expanded sections, a FAQ accordion, or a filters panel. The user set up their view intentionally, and restoring it avoids re-doing that work.
A dropdown menu or popover triggered by a button click. These are transient interactions, not persistent view state. Returning to a page with a dropdown already open is not user friendly.

Activity preserves form input values (text fields, selected options, checkbox states), submission results, and status messages across navigations.
A search page with filters, a draft the user was composing, or a settings form with unsaved changes. Preserving input state is one of the biggest UX wins because the user doesn't lose work.

You can use a callback ref to call

<form
	ref={(form) => {
		return () => form?.reset()

This resets all fields whenever the user navigates away.

Page-level styles (CSS variables, z-index, global classes) can affect visible pages when the originating component is hidden by Activity. You likely want to disable them when hidden: a hidden page's accent color or z-index overrides shouldn't leak into the visible page.
Use a callback ref to toggle the stylesheet's

<style
	ref={(style) => {
		if (style) style.media = '' // Enable when visible
		return () => {
			if (style) style.media = 'not all' // Disable when hidden
		}
	}}>
	{`:root { --page-accent: blue; }`}
</style>

but remains in the document. This applies both to routes preserved by Cache Components and to content you hide with
directly. It affects end-to-end testing with tools like Playwright, Cypress, or Puppeteer:
DOM queries can find hidden elements.
Selectors may match elements regardless of visibility.
Interactions with hidden elements fail or time out.

Most tools wait for an element to become visible before interacting, but waiting doesn't narrow a query that matches both a visible and a hidden element. Playwright reports this as a strict mode violation.
Be explicit about visibility when asserting element presence.
Prefer locators that query the accessibility tree, which leaves out hidden elements, or filter matches by visibility before acting on them. In Playwright,
queries exclude hidden elements by default:
, can match hidden elements. Filter them by visibility explicitly:

// Filter by visibility explicitly
await page.getByLabel('Email').filter({ visible: true }).fill('test@example.com')
await page.getByPlaceholder('Search...').filter({ visible: true }).fill('query')
await page.locator('.product-card').filter({ visible: true }).first().click()
await page.locator('[data-testid="timer"]').filter({ visible: true }).textContent()

// Avoid - may match hidden elements in Activity boundaries
await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('test@example.com')
await page.locator('.product-card').first().click()

is robust to Activity, tabbed navigation, accordions, and any other pattern that keeps hidden content in the DOM. It queries the accessibility tree, which excludes hidden elements. Which locators match hidden elements varies between testing tools and their versions, so check your tool's documentation for its locators and test helpers to confirm.
Cache Components uses Activity automatically at the route level, but you can also use
directly in your own components. This is useful for tabs, expandable panels, or any UI where you want to hide content without unmounting it.
Activity can prerender content the user hasn't seen yet. Hidden boundaries render at lower priority. Combined with Suspense, this lets you prefetch data for content the user is likely to view next.
